title: Haemolysis by collection method and site: choosing between a systematic review and a local laboratory data study
subtitle: Design not yet settled: a systematic review of collection method or a retrospective laboratory data study
statement: Emergency department potassium samples haemolyse at about five times the ward rate (8.1 against 1.5 percent), causing rejected results, repeat draws and delays. Emergency samples differ from ward samples in collection method (cannula rather than needle), collector (nurses rather than phlebotomists) and transport (pneumatic tube rather than hand-carried). The emergency department wants to keep cannula draws to spare patients a second needle stick. The laboratory needs to decide whether a policy on collection method is justified, and by which kind of study.
whoAffected: Emergency patients, especially children and people with difficult veins; emergency nurses and physicians; laboratory staff who reject and repeat samples.
whatHurts: Rejected potassium results delay decisions and cause repeat needle sticks; a policy banning cannula draws would add needle sticks for the patients least able to tolerate them.
currentPractice: Cannula draws with standard vacuum tubes by emergency nurses; high-speed pneumatic tube transport; rejection or comment on haemolysed samples; no routine monitoring by collection site.
whyNow: Emergency physicians are pressing the laboratory about delays, and the directors must jointly decide any policy change.
constraints: No research funding; the laboratory quality lead and one biochemistry trainee can give about 80 hours between them before June 2027; any change to emergency department collection policy needs the joint approval of the emergency and laboratory directors.
patientCenteredGoal: Emergency patients get reliable potassium results from a single needle stick whenever possible.
summary: Problem framed; the design is left unresolved between a systematic review and a local retrospective study until the evidence is reviewed.
